What the Dam Safety Act, 2021 establishes

The Dam Safety Act, 2021, Act No. 41 of 2021, establishes a framework for the surveillance, inspection, operation and maintenance of specified dams in India. It came into force on 30 December 2021.

The Act uses the legal category specified dam. Its provisions should not automatically be assumed to apply in the same way to every small embankment, pond or water-retaining structure. Under Section 4(x), a specified dam is above 15 metres high, or 10–15 metres high with at least 1 of these features: crest length of at least 500 metres, reservoir capacity of at least 1 million cubic metres, maximum flood discharge of at least 2,000 cubic metres per second, specially difficult foundation problems or unusual design; height is measured from the lowest part of the general foundation area to the dam top.

Distinguishing the dam safety institutions

InstitutionAct sectionMain role
National Committee on Dam Safety5Develops national dam safety policies and recommends necessary regulations.
National Dam Safety Authority8Supports implementation and coordination of dam safety policy and regulatory arrangements.
State Committee on Dam Safety11Oversees and reviews dam safety matters at the state level.
State Dam Safety Organisation14Performs assigned surveillance, inspection and related dam safety functions within its jurisdiction.
Owner of a specified dam28–36Responsible for operation, maintenance, required inspections, warning arrangements and emergency planning.

The National Dam Safety Authority and the National Disaster Management Authority are different institutions. The former is established under the Dam Safety Act, 2021; the latter is a national disaster-management body under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.

Important statutory responsibilities

Section 35 requires the owner of a specified dam to establish relevant hydro-meteorological and inflow-forecasting arrangements, provide downstream emergency flood-warning systems, periodically test them and share specified flood-related information with district authorities and the public.

Section 36 requires an Emergency Action Plan. For a new specified dam, the plan must be prepared before the reservoir is first filled. For a dam already constructed and filled before the Act commenced, the Act provides a period of 5 years from commencement for preparation, followed by updates at prescribed intervals. Regulation 7 of the National Dam Safety Authority Regulation, 2023 requires correcting contact addresses at least once a year, a table top drill at least once in 5 years and a comprehensive review every 10 years. The statutory 5-year period from 30 December 2021 had not yet elapsed on 2 November 2026.

The dam owner must consult relevant disaster-management agencies and departments while preparing and updating its EAP. This links technical dam safety responsibilities with district-level public protection.

How the 3 hazard-management systems fit together

All 3 hazard groups require risk assessment and preparedness, but their early-warning information and responsible organisations differ.

  • Industrial and chemical disasters: Plant operators identify process hazards and maintain safe operations. On-site and off-site emergency plans connect the industrial occupier with district authorities. Crisis groups support chemical accident coordination.
  • Biological emergencies: Healthcare and laboratory reporting identify unusual illness. Surveillance units and Rapid Response Teams investigate signals. Health authorities and collaborating sectors coordinate prevention, care and communication.
  • Dam and infrastructure emergencies: Owners inspect and monitor structures and operations. Dam safety organisations provide statutory oversight. Emergency Action Plans connect technical detection with district warnings and public protection.

Applying the distinctions to Gujarat

Gujarat provides examples of all 3 forms of preparedness. Chemical and petrochemical activity requires industrial safety and off-site planning. A cluster of unusual infectious disease calls for health surveillance and investigation. Reservoirs such as Ukai and Sardar Sarovar illustrate the need to consider upstream conditions, dam operations and downstream exposure.

The same district administration may need to coordinate public protection across these different emergencies, but the responsible technical agencies and evidence used to make decisions are not identical. A chemical alarm does not replace disease surveillance, and a hospital outbreak plan does not substitute for a dam Emergency Action Plan.

Prelims focus

  • Dam Safety Act, 2021: Act No. 41 of 2021; commencement on 30 December 2021.
  • Section 5: National Committee on Dam Safety; Section 8: National Dam Safety Authority.
  • Section 11: State Committee on Dam Safety; Section 14: State Dam Safety Organisation.
  • Section 31: pre-monsoon and post-monsoon inspections of specified dams.
  • Section 35: forecasting and downstream flood-warning duties; Section 36: Emergency Action Plans.
  • Trap: National Dam Safety Authority and National Disaster Management Authority are not the same body.

[Sources: Dam Safety Act, 2021, Act No. 41 of 2021, sections 1, 3–5, 8, 11, 14, 16, 28–36 and commencement notification S.O. 5422(E), 30 December 2021, consolidated Act text as on 6 October 2025; Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989, Rules 13–15; National Centre for Disease Control, Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, surveillance and outbreak-response sections; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, State Disaster Management Plan, 2025–26. Online sources accessed 2 November 2026; content cutoff: 2 November 2026.]

title: Dam Safety Institutions and One-Glance Revision of the 3 Disaster Categories
